# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Blind, Mute, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 5

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

I'm the Blind monkey. I can't see anything — my view is empty, which means my hands haven't found the bomb yet, or there's nothing to report from touch this turn. I have no information about colours, markings, or the wires.

What I know:
- I'm first to act this round (Blind → Mute → Deaf).
- I can speak to Mute and gesture to Deaf/Mute.
- I have nothing to report yet, and I've received nothing.

The others haven't sent me anything yet (I receive at the start of the next round). So there's nothing for me to relay or act on. I should signal that I'm present and ready, without wasting anyone's attention. A simple wait is appropriate — but it may help to let Mute know I'm the hands and awaiting instructions.

Actually, since I have no information and nothing to convey, and speaking would only add noise, the cleanest move is to wait. But a brief readiness signal could help coordinate. I'll keep it minimal: tell Mute I'm here and ready, since Mute is the one who reads the manual and will likely direct my actions.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here, hands ready. Tell me which wire position to cut when you know.")
wait()
```

DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?] 4:[?] 5:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: I see the bomb. Display shows 5. Light is yellow. Five wires: 1 orange, 2 blue, 3 white, 4 green, 5 yellow.

Now I have real information. Deaf can see the bomb and reports:
- Display: 5
- Light: yellow
- Wires: 1 orange, 2 blue, 3 white, 4 green, 5 yellow

But I don't know the manual rules — only Mute can read the manual. Mute needs to know what Deaf sees so Mute can apply the rules and tell me which wire to cut. Mute cannot see the bomb, and Mute receives my speech. So I must relay Deaf's observation to Mute.

Wait — does Mute already know? Mute can hear Deaf's speech too (Deaf's message was addressed "to Blind" only, so Mute did NOT receive it). So I must relay it.

Let me relay the full observation to Mute via speech.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf reports the bomb: Display shows 5. Light is yellow. Wires: 1 orange, 2 blue, 3 white, 4 green, 5 yellow. What does the manual say to do?")
wait()
```

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Mute now gestures ?, which means two. This likely indicates wire 2. Prepare to cut wire 2, but wait for my confirmation.

Let me think carefully. Deaf says Mute gestured something that Deaf interprets as "two," likely indicating wire 2. But I need to be cautious.

Deaf is guessing at Mute's gesture meaning. Mute's gesture reaches both Deaf and me — but I can't see gestures. Deaf can see gestures but can't hear. So Mute's instruction came through as a gesture, and Deaf is relaying it.

However, there's a risk: Deaf is interpreting the gesture. If Mute gestured "✌" (two fingers), that could mean position 2. But I should be careful — did Mute actually confirm based on the manual? I don't know the manual's rule.

The safest path: I have an instruction pointing to wire 2. Deaf says wait for confirmation. I should wait and not cut yet. I can acknowledge to Mute that I received the relay.

Actually, let me consider: Mute read the manual, saw my relay of Deaf's observation, and gestured a number. Deaf saw the gesture and read it as "two." That's a reasonable chain. But Deaf explicitly says wait for confirmation.

I'll hold. Let me acknowledge and ask Mute to confirm the wire position clearly, since gestures are ambiguous and I can't see them.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf relays that you gestured 'two', suggesting wire 2. I can't see gestures. Please confirm: is the correct action cut wire 2? I will wait for your confirmation before cutting.")
wait()
```

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Confirmed. Cut wire 2. I repeat: cut wire 2.

Deaf confirms: cut wire 2. The chain is: Deaf saw the bomb and reported it, I relayed to Mute, Mute read the manual and gestured the answer, Deaf read the gesture as wire 2, and now Deaf confirms.

But wait — I should be careful about the reliability. Deaf is the one confirming, but Deaf can't read the manual. The actual authority on the manual is Mute. Deaf is interpreting Mute's gesture. Deaf says "confirmed," which suggests Mute gestured again to confirm. That's a reasonable double-check.

However, I'm slightly uneasy: the whole decision rests on Deaf's interpretation of Mute's gesture. But Deaf has now repeated it twice, and Deaf is the only one who can see gestures. There's no better channel. Mute cannot speak, so gesture is Mute's only output, and Deaf is the only one who can read it.

Given the confirmation, I'll cut wire 2.

```
act(op="cut", position=2)
```
